spoken_notes: Welcome everyone. In this briefing, we are walking through our production Google Cloud implementation of Zero-Bloat MCP Gateway: Dynamic Top-K Tool Search + RFC 8693 OAuth 2.1 On-Behalf-Of Security, grounded directly on IETF RFC 8693 OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange + MCP Dynamic Tool Discovery Specification.

We have organized this session into three clear acts: first, the enterprise problem and architectural options across Slides 1 to 3; second, a top-down L1 through L4 architectural deep dive across Slides 4 to 7; and third, our fail-closed verification gates and one-click Terraform deployment across Slides 8 to 12.
Let us start by examining the exact production failure modes this architecture solves and the primary-source evidence backing our design.

slides.header_breadcrumb: ACT I • CUSTOMER USE CASES & PRIMARY-SOURCE EVIDENCE
slides.headline: Grounded Problem Statement & Verified Primary-Source Proofs
slides.subtitle: Primary Technical Artifact: IETF RFC 8693 OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange + MCP Dynamic Tool Discovery Specification (urn:ietf:rfc:8693:mcp-zero-bloat-gateway-2026)

cards.title: Primary-Source Mechanism 1
cards.body: Preloading 85 enterprise MCP tool schemas consumes 55,240 prompt tokens/turn ($0.420) and degrades tool selection accuracy to 61.0%; hybrid BM25 + dense top-K (K=4) discovery trims active schemas to 1,380 tokens (-97.5%, $0.014/turn) while keeping the L1 prefix cache 100% frozen.

cards.title: Primary-Source Mechanism 2
cards.body: RFC 8693 On-Behalf-Of (OBO) STS token exchange swaps the caller's short-lived OIDC assertion for an audience-scoped (`aud=mcp://tool`), 300-second per-user JWT so zero static downstream admin keys ever reside in agent memory.

cards.title: Primary-Source Mechanism 3
cards.body: Cryptographic state-token HMAC/ECDSA verification + tenant ACL enforcement rejects forged or cross-tenant Confused-Deputy tool invocations in 0.4ms (HTTP 400/403) before any downstream mutation executes.

cards.title: Unified Google Cloud Stack
cards.body: Google Cloud ADK MCPToolset • Cloud IAM Security Token Service (RFC 8693 OBO) • Vertex AI Gemini 4 Argon & 3.8 Flash (locations/global) • Google Cloud Model Armor

spoken_notes: Building on our opening overview, this slide grounds our architecture in verified primary-source evidence rather than unverified industry hype.

Specifically, Preloading 85 enterprise MCP tool schemas consumes 55,240 prompt tokens/turn ($0.420) and degrades tool selection accuracy to 61.0%; hybrid BM25 + dense top-K (K=4) discovery trims active schemas to 1,380 tokens (-97.5%, $0.014/turn) while keeping the L1 prefix cache 100% frozen. Furthermore, RFC 8693 On-Behalf-Of (OBO) STS token exchange swaps the caller's short-lived OIDC assertion for an audience-scoped (`aud=mcp://tool`), 300-second per-user JWT so zero static downstream admin keys ever reside in agent memory.
With these three foundational mechanisms established, let us look at how we evaluate architectural patterns before locking in our target Google Cloud topology.

slides.header_breadcrumb: ACT I • ARCHITECTURAL OPTIONS & PATTERN A/B/C TRADE-OFF MATRIX
slides.headline: Evaluating Static Prompts vs. Unverified Agents vs. OpenHands + ADK
slides.subtitle: 3-Stage Evolution: Pattern A (Static BMAD Prompts) -> Pattern B (Unguarded Tool Loop) -> Pattern C (ADK + OpenHands Sandbox)

cards.title: Static Meta-Prompts (BMAD)
cards.body: Generates unverified markdown templates; zero runtime test execution and high hallucination drift.

cards.title: Unguarded LLM Tool Loop
cards.body: Direct tool access without channel isolation, deterministic checkpoints, or regression gates.

cards.title: Google ADK + OpenHands Sandbox
cards.body: Autonomous container execution with Vertex AI Gemini (locations/global) and 100% test-gated commits.

cards.title: Enterprise Selection Standard
cards.body: Enforce Pattern C across all production workloads to guarantee zero unverified code or memory drift.

spoken_notes: Now that we understand the primary-source requirements, teams typically ask why they cannot solve this with static prompt templates or a basic chatbot loop.

As shown in Pattern A and Pattern B, static markdown templates like BMAD never execute code in a real sandbox, and unguarded tool loops expose enterprise systems to regressions and prompt injection. Pattern C combines Google Cloud ADK with OpenHands sandboxed verification so every change is tested before commit.
Next, let us zoom into Act II and inspect the L1 logical trust boundaries that enforce Pattern C in production.

spoken_notes: Entering Act II, we start at Level 1—the logical three-zone trust boundary view of our Google Cloud architecture.

Zone 1 handles authenticated request ingress and context normalization. Zone 2 runs the stateless Cloud Run ADK orchestrator and OpenHands sandbox worker. Zone 3 houses our governance gates and CMEK-encrypted data stores inside a VPC Service Controls perimeter.

slides.header_breadcrumb: ACT II • L3 PROCESS CHRONOLOGICAL 6-STAGE LIFELINE
slides.headline: Monotonic 6-Step Execution Sequence & Fail-Closed Guardrails
slides.subtitle: Chronological Happy-Path Lifeline (Steps 01..06) with Deterministic Verification Checkpoints

cards.title: Authenticate Caller OIDC
cards.body: Validate end-user OIDC JWT and extract explicit tenant_id and principal claims at ingress.

cards.title: Lazy Hybrid Top-K Search & RFC 8693 OBO Token Swap
cards.body: Query BM25 + dense embeddings across 85+ registered MCP tools and mount only top-4 slim schemas (1,380 tokens). Exchange caller assertion via Cloud IAM STS for a 300s per-user token scoped strictly to `aud=mcp://<selected_tool>`.

cards.title: Model Armor & Tamper Check & Scoped MCP Tool Execution
cards.body: Screen tool arguments for indirect prompt injection and verify cryptographic state-token signature + tenant match. Invoke downstream Cloud Run / FastMCP server using the short-lived user-delegated OBO credential.

cards.title: Emit SHA-256 Audit Receipt
cards.body: Persist immutable SHA-256 execution receipt to Spanner and enforce the 72-case CI regression gate.

spoken_notes: Slide 6 maps the Level 3 chronological sequence across all six execution stages.

The flow begins with Authenticate Caller OIDC and progresses through Lazy Hybrid Top-K Search and RFC 8693 OBO Token Swap. Before any output or commit is finalized, Stages 4 through 6 enforce Scoped MCP Tool Execution and Emit SHA-256 Audit Receipt.
Now let us inspect the exact Level 4 wire payload transformation that occurs inside these hops on Slide 7.

slides.header_breadcrumb: ACT II • L4 WIRE 3-STAGE PAYLOAD & GUARDRAIL TRANSFORMATION
slides.headline: Wire-Level Envelope Isolation & Cryptographic Receipt Binding
slides.subtitle: Incoming Raw Signal (#D93025) -> ADK & Model Armor Normalization (#1B5E7B) -> Verified Grounded Artifact (#1E8E3E)

cards.title: Unverified Input Payload
cards.body: Untrusted external document, unverified memory claim, or raw task brief entering the gateway.

cards.title: ADK + Model Armor Envelope
cards.body: Separates system instructions from data channels, attaches SHA-256 evidence receipts, and scopes tool JWTs.

cards.title: Certified Output & Receipt
cards.body: Emits schema-validated JSON payload with kms_ecdsa_p256 signature and 100% test-verified status.

cards.title: Zero Hallucination Contract
cards.body: Payloads lacking a valid primary-source receipt or failing sandbox tests are rejected deterministically.

spoken_notes: Completing Act II, Slide 7 shows the Level 4 wire-level payload transformation across three stages.

Raw inputs—whether external documents or candidate code diffs—are never trusted implicitly. The normalization engine wraps data in isolated envelopes, verifies cryptographic version receipts, and only emits the Stage 3 payload once all policy assertions pass.
With the L1 through L4 architecture defined, let us move into Act III on Slide 8 to examine our failure recovery and circuit breaker pipelines.

slides.header_breadcrumb: ACT III • DETERMINISTIC FAIL-CLOSED CIRCUIT BREAKERS & FEEDBACK LOOP
slides.headline: Four-Node Circuit Breaker & Self-Healing Closed-Loop State Machine
slides.subtitle: Node 1: Detect Drift/Failure -> Node 2: Quarantine & Replay -> Node 3: Synthesize Fix -> Node 4: Re-Verify & Promote

cards.title: Deterministic Anomaly Trigger
cards.body: Catches stale SHA receipts, prompt injection tokens, or failing unit tests in O(1) time.

cards.title: Fail-Closed Isolation
cards.body: Quarantines untrusted claims or broken diffs so they never reach downstream production consumers.

cards.title: OpenHands + Gemini Repair
cards.body: Synthesizes minimal bounded remediation inside an isolated container sandbox.

cards.title: Regression Gate & Loop Return
cards.body: Re-runs full verification suite and feeds telemetry back to Node 1 for continuous protection.

spoken_notes: In Act III, we focus on resilience under adversarial or changing conditions. Slide 8 illustrates our four-node circuit breaker state machine.

Whenever a code change invalidates an existing memory receipt or a test fails in the sandbox, Node 1 triggers immediately, Node 2 quarantines the affected path, Node 3 invokes our repair loop, and Node 4 blocks promotion until the full regression suite passes.
